title: Rails service objects with a result you can trust
outcome: Define inputs, results, transaction ownership, and error policy for one Rails use case.
useCase: A use case shared by controllers and imports.
drawbacks: Too many forwarding-only services can add indirection.
cue: A service name is not a guarantee. Write the contract.

trace.title: Trusted input
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

A service object is ordinary Ruby. It earns its place by naming one use case and making its boundary clear.

It does not automatically supply permissions, a transaction, retries, or thread safety.

Choose a result contract. A business rejection such as “already closed” can be an expected result.

An unexpected database or programmer error should remain visible to monitoring. Do not rescue everything into nil; callers then cannot tell rejection from failure.

State who owns the transaction and which side effects happen later. Keep request-specific data in arguments and local values.

Class-level mutable state can leak across calls or threads.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Controller validates permitted input and identifies actor → service checks the use-case rule → transaction writes → result maps to HTTP.

A job caller uses the same rule with a deliberate actor/system role.

Unit-test expected branches with a narrow seam. Use database tests for rollback and constraints.

Test the caller’s mapping so a failure is not shown as a success response.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: A service that catches StandardError and returns success hides operational defects. Passing a model from a controller does not mean it belongs to the actor’s tenant.
